formula: Affirmative: S + V₁ / V_s/es + O | Negative: S + do/does not + V₁ + O
auxiliary: None in affirmative; do / does in negative & interrogative
usage: Habitual actions, universal/scientific truths, permanent facts, scheduled future routines.

patterns.affirmative: The High Court issues notices on Mondays.
patterns.negative: The High Court does not issue notices on Sundays.
patterns.interrogative: Does the High Court issue notices on Mondays?

keyTip: Use V_s/es ONLY with 3rd-person singular affirmative subjects. Contextual note: frequency adverbs like 'always' can take Present Continuous to express irritation/annoyance (e.g., 'He is always interrupting').

usage: Actions actively taking place right at the moment of speaking, or temporary ongoing situations.

patterns.affirmative: The system assistant is configuring the server right now.
patterns.negative: The system assistant is not configuring the server at present.
patterns.interrogative: Is the system assistant configuring the server right now?

keyTip: Avoid using continuous aspect with stative verbs (know, believe, understand, belong, possess). Note that 'always' can combine with continuous aspect to indicate annoyance.

usage: Completed past action with direct present relevance, or unspecified past life experience.

patterns.affirmative: The registrar has verified the electronic documents.
patterns.negative: The registrar has not verified the electronic documents yet.
patterns.interrogative: Has the registrar verified the electronic documents yet?

keyTip: FATAL EXAM TRAP: NEVER pair Present Perfect with definite past time markers (yesterday, ago, in 2021).

formula: Subject + has/have + been + V_ing + Object + since/for + Time
usage: Action that began at a point in the past and continues without interruption into the present moment.

patterns.affirmative: The IT department has been testing the software for three hours.
patterns.negative: The IT department has not been testing the software since morning.
patterns.interrogative: Has the IT department been testing the software for three hours?

keyTip: 'Since' marks a starting point; 'for' marks duration. Contextual distinction: a completed period takes Simple Past ('He worked in Jaipur for three years'), while an ongoing period extending to the present uses Present Perfect or Perfect Continuous ('He has worked here for three years').

formula: Affirmative: S + V₂ + O | Negative: S + did not + V₁ + O
auxiliary: None in affirmative; did in negative & interrogative
usage: Completed action that took place at a definite, finished point or period in the past.

patterns.affirmative: The bench pronounced the verdict yesterday.
patterns.negative: The bench did not pronounce the verdict yesterday.
patterns.interrogative: Did the bench pronounce the verdict yesterday?

keyTip: In affirmative clauses, V₂ is the past lexical verb form (no auxiliary). In negative and interrogative clauses, 'did' is the auxiliary and takes lexical base V₁ ('did not see', never 'did not saw'). If an action was in progress at a past point ('at 4 PM yesterday'), use Past Continuous.

usage: Action ongoing at a specific moment in the past, or continuous background to a past reference time.

patterns.affirmative: The clerk was updating the database at 4 PM yesterday.
patterns.negative: The clerk was not updating the database at that time.
patterns.interrogative: Was the clerk updating the database at 4 PM yesterday?

keyTip: Specifies an action in progress at a specific past moment. Note: 'yesterday' alone typically takes Simple Past, but a specific moment in progress ('at 4 PM yesterday') takes Past Continuous.

usage: An action completed prior to a specific past reference point or boundary.

patterns.affirmative: The witness had left the courtroom by 11 AM.
patterns.negative: The witness had not left the courtroom by 11 AM.
patterns.interrogative: Had the witness left the courtroom by 11 AM?

keyTip: Earlier Past Action = Past Perfect (had + V₃) relative to a past reference point. Advanced cross-clause sequence of tenses between two past actions is deferred to Lesson 02.

formula: Subject + had + been + V_ing + Object + since/for + Time
usage: Ongoing action that had been occurring for a duration prior to a specific reference point in the past.

patterns.affirmative: They had been troubleshooting the network for two hours before noon.
patterns.negative: They had not been monitoring the servers since morning.
patterns.interrogative: Had they been troubleshooting the network for two hours before noon?

keyTip: Emphasizes duration leading directly up to a past reference point. Multi-clause sequence of tenses is developed in Lesson 02.

auxiliary: will (all subjects) / shall (traditionally 1st-person I/we in formal English)
usage: Spontaneous decisions, predictions, promises, or future scheduled occurrences.

patterns.affirmative: The committee will release the notification tomorrow.
patterns.negative: The committee will not release the notification tomorrow.
patterns.interrogative: Will the committee release the notification tomorrow?

keyTip: In legal/official documents, 'shall' denotes mandatory obligation rather than simple futurity.

usage: Action that will be actively in progress at a specific temporal point in the future.

patterns.affirmative: The candidates will be writing their exam at 10 AM tomorrow.
patterns.negative: The candidates will not be writing their exam at that hour.
patterns.interrogative: Will the candidates be writing their exam at 10 AM tomorrow?

keyTip: Future Continuous cannot be transformed into passive voice in standard English.

formula: Subject + will/shall + have + V₃ + Object + by + Time
usage: Action that will be completely finished before or by a specified deadline in the future.

patterns.affirmative: The administration will have digitized all records by the end of this year.
patterns.negative: The administration will not have digitized all records by then.
patterns.interrogative: Will the administration have digitized all records by the end of this year?

timeMarkers: by the time + Simple Present clause
keyTip: Whenever you see 'by + future time', Future Perfect ('will have + V₃') is the standard completion form.

formula: Subject + will/shall + have + been + V_ing + for + Duration + by + Time
auxiliary: will have been / shall have been
usage: Action that will have been continuously occurring for an ongoing duration up to a specified future landmark.

patterns.affirmative: By next July, he will have been serving as System Assistant for five years.
patterns.negative: By next July, he will not have been serving here for that long.
patterns.interrogative: Will he have been serving for five years by next July?

keyTip: Combines a completion deadline ('by...') with an ongoing duration measurement ('for...').
